newsitem.title: INDIA: India weighs options to rein in galloping oil bill.
newsitem.headline: India weighs options to rein in galloping oil bill.

text.p: India, faced with a huge oil subsidy bill, is weighing options including the phased decontrol of products prices but is unlikely to hurry the politically sensitive step, officials and analysts said on Monday.
Petroleum Ministry officials said Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who also holds the petroleum portfolio, was briefed during the weekend on ways to contain the subsidies.
The options included phased dismantling of the administered price mechanism (APM) on oil products, they said.
"There was a presentation on Saturday on the APM to the Prime Minister," a petroleum ministry official told Reuters.
The official said the issue might be taken up by Deve Gowda and his cabinet colleagues at a meeting on Tuesday.
India's crude oil and petroleum products prices are administered by the government. Farmers and low-income groups are supplied diesel and kerosene at subsidised rates.
A government-appointed panel last September had suggested a phased decontrolling of the oil sector by the year 2002.

It said the first phase should begin between 1996 and 1998 and cover rationalisation of the tariff structure, deregulation of natural gas pricing and of furnace oil and bitumen, and partial decontrol of marketing.

The panel, headed by the highest ranking civil servant in the ministry of petroleum and natural gas, suggested removal of subsidies on high speed diesel and a cut in subsidies on kerosene, LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) and inputs for fertilisers.

Petroleum ministry officials said the total subsidy on petroleum products in 1996/97 (April-March) was estimated at 184 billion rupees ($5.1 billion), including 83 billion rupees on kerosene and 64 billion on diesel.
"Kerosene and diesel are items on which removal of subsidies have been proposed. If it comes they (government) don't have to review the prices since it will become market-related," said one official.
Opinions differ on whether the government will grasp the nettle and increase the price of kerosene, the fuel used by India's poor for cooking and lighting.
"I don't think they can take a step to remove the subsidy on kerosene but maybe they can reduce it," said Anushri Sinha of the independent National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).
Former finance minister Manmohan Singh said in a newspaper interview on Monday that India cannot continue to have the present administered price system for petroleum products.
"We have to deregulate. But we cannot do it overnight and cannot put the entire burden of deregulation on the consumers."
Officials at the Prime Minister's office said any immediate decision on measures to contain the subsidy bill were not likely, given the nature of the centre-left coalition.

They said any increase in petroleum prices at this time would be unpopular and erase the positive effect of the government's 1997/98 (April-March) federal budget which has been hailed as market-friendly.
Deve Gowda's government raised petroleum prices shortly after taking office last June, sparking a row among the partners in the fragile 15-party ruling coalition.
India's oil pool deficit, effectively the amount government owes oil companies for selling prdoducts well below world prices, is expected to hit 158 billion rupees by the end of March.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his budget speech on February 28 dodged the major issue of how to finance subsidised oil prices and omitted expected cuts in oil import tariffs.
